world.title: Environmental impacts, surveillance and mitigation of antimicrobial resistance
world.description: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major barrier to achieving Sustainable Development Goals. The environment has a crucial role in AMR development and transmission. In this Review, we summarize global patterns of AMR distribution in the environment and explore its key sources and drivers. Analyses of global environmental metagenomes reveal that water serves as the main transmission pathway for bacterial genetic elements encoding AMR, with sewage representing the largest contributor, followed by freshwater systems, whereas soil has a comparatively minor role. Given the complex nature of microbiomes and antibiotic resistance genes across different environments, systematic surveillance is key to understanding the evolution and spread of AMR. To address methodological differences across environmental AMR studies, we propose a standardized metagenomic approach for the establishment of an integrated surveillance framework. Within this framework, a minimal strategy maximizes limited resources to achieve basic surveillance, whereas a comprehensive strategy allocates resources for in-depth profiling. Characterization of the environmental resistome will identify regional challenges and help to design mitigation strategies. We advocate for systematic environmental surveillance to monitor AMR, with a view to improve understanding of its sources and transmission, and to support the scale-up of integrated AMR management worldwide. The environment has an important role in the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This Review discusses the global patterns of AMR distribution and sources and drivers of AMR, and it proposes a standardized surveillance framework to support integrated monitoring, risk assessment and mitigation efforts worldwide.

business.title: Work-family bidirectional conflicts and their impact on working mothers’ job satisfaction in Bangladesh
business.description: In recent decades, the employment rates of married women have risen markedly on a global scale. Bangladesh, a South Asian country with a burgeoning economy and a population of 164 million, has witnessed a rise in women’s engagement in the labour market over the years. The majority of women in Bangladesh get married before or after they start their working lives. The struggle of these working mothers to balance their work and family lives becomes increasingly complicated, consequently diminishing their job satisfaction. The primary assumption made throughout this study is that time and stress are the leading predictors of work-family conflicts in both directions, i.e., from family-to-work and work-to-family, which influence the level of job satisfaction among working mothers. The analysis is predicated on a sample of 307 full-time employed mothers with at least one child under the age of 8. Findings indicate that both time-based and strain-based family-to-work conflict (FWC_TB and FWC_SB) and strain-based work-to-family conflict (WFC_SB) have a significant and adverse impact on the job satisfaction of working mothers in Bangladesh. Conversely, our study demonstrates no substantial effect of time-based work-to-family conflicts (WFC_TB) on the job satisfaction of working mothers. Thus, the current research simultaneously supports and contradicts the prevailing literature on work-to-family conflict (WFC) and family-to-work conflict (FWC). The present study advances the existing literature by addressing the lacuna in our nuanced understanding of how time-based and strain-based WFC and FWC affect the level of job satisfaction for working mothers, particularly in the context of developing countries. This study recommends that organisations and management adopt strategies and conduct counselling for working mothers to integrate their family and work time, reduce family and work-related strains and consequently, enhance their job satisfaction level.

science.title: Attractive and repulsive couplings between circadian pacemaker neurons promote entrainment to light-dark cycles with after-effect
science.description: The mammalian circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), comprises a core region that receives light signals from the retina and a shell region that outputs pacemaking rhythms to peripheral tissues. The free-running period (FRP) of animals in constant darkness (DD) correlates with the period of the preceding LD cycle, a phenomenon known as after-effect. To elucidate the mechanisms underlying robust entrainment and after-effect, we analyzed phase oscillator models incorporating attractive and repulsive couplings that respectively decrease or increase phase differences between oscillators. Attractive coupling from the core to shell regions accounts for experimentally observed phase relationships between these regions under LD cycles. Remarkably, repulsive coupling from the shell to core regions promotes SCN entrainability to LD cycles. Furthermore, after transfer to DD, the FRP slowly returns to the intrinsic SCN period, reflecting the after-effect. Our analysis identifies an SCN coupling architecture that underlies stable daily activity rhythms.

science.title: Explainable and uncertainty-calibrated stacked ensemble for predicting compressive strength of blended cementitious concrete
science.description: Accurate and transparent prediction of concrete compressive strength can support rapid screening of candidate mixture designs. This study develops an explainable, uncertainty-aware workflow that combines domain-informed features, including the water-to-binder ratio (w/b), superplasticizer-to-binder ratio (SP/b), and supplementary cementitious material fractions, with a stacked ensemble tuned using hybrid genetic algorithm–particle swarm optimisation (GA–PSO). Random Forest, XGBoost, and a shallow feed-forward neural network are combined through an Elastic–Net meta-regressor trained using out-of-fold base-model predictions. The analysis uses the public Yeh concrete compressive-strength dataset, comprising 1030 original records and 1005 records retained after documented data-integrity screening. Model development used age-stratified 10-fold cross-validation within an 80% modelling partition, while a disjoint 20% hold-out partition was excluded from model development and used for final evaluation. The stacked ensemble achieved an internal cross-validation RMSE of 2.485 MPa, MAE of 1.201 MPa, and R2 = 0.941. On the untouched hold-out set, the corresponding values were 2.62 MPa, 1.27 MPa, and 0.936. Relative to GA–PSO-tuned XGBoost, the hold-out RMSE decreased from 5.05 to 2.62 MPa. Paired bootstrap resampling of the hold-out observations gave a 95% RMSE interval of [2.33, 2.96] MPa for the stack compared with [4.44, 5.66] MPa for tuned XGBoost. MC-dropout and residual-bootstrap uncertainty intervals showed near-nominal empirical coverage, while SHAP and Morris analyses consistently identified w/b, curing age, cement content, and SP/b as influential predictors. These findings establish strong internal predictive performance on the historical Yeh dataset; external validation on contemporary and project-specific concrete data is required before practical engineering use.
